blocks.text: 6.5.5 Jurisdictional and Portfolio Minimum/Maximum Spend

GridCap's rate case comes back from the regulator with a set of spending rules for the small portfolio's five-year plan. Each year's capital budget is a ceiling, as before. But the utility also promised to *use* its budget: a plan that leaves money unspent will be read as a sign the budget was too high. Each of the four regions (the **jurisdictions**: areas with their own regulator, municipality or rate base) was promised a minimum over the plan. And the board wants vegetation work to be at least a fixed share of the plan, and transmission at most half of it. Every one of these is a bound on money spent, from above or from below, on the whole **portfolio** or on a slice of it. This lesson writes them as rows on the spend expressions the model already has, shows what floors do to a plan, and checks them before the solve, in four rules.

GridCap is a fictional utility's portfolio, generated for this course. Its regional floors (`region_floor`) are part of the data; the yearly floors, the raised Plains floor and the shares below are invented for the lesson.
A Spend Limit Is a Row on a Spend Expression, From Above or From Below
Lesson 6.4.2 built the plan's spend in year $`y`$ as a linear expression of the start variables, with each project's cost spread over the years it is worked on:
\text{spend}_y = \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t}

The budget row is a ceiling on it, $`\text{spend}_y \le B_y`$. A **floor** is the same expression bounded from below. Two are common: a yearly floor, at least a share $`\alpha`$ of each year's budget, and a floor on the plan as a whole, which lets the plan spend less in one year if it spends more in another:

\text{spend}_y \ge \alpha B_y \quad \forall y \in Y \quad \text{(floor}_y), \qquad
\sum_{y \in Y} \text{spend}_y \ge \alpha \sum_{y \in Y} B_y \quad \text{(floor\_plan)}
`portfolio_spend.py` solves GridCap small with each floor and prints the NPV, the plan's total spend and the share of each year's budget it uses:

Without a floor the plan already spends 98% or more of every year's budget: projects are lumpy, and the last few hundred thousand dollars of a year rarely buy a whole project. Each floor closes part of that gap and costs NPV, and the cost grows fast. A 99% floor in every year costs $174k. Spending every last dollar ($`\alpha = 1`$, which turns each budget row into an equality) costs $5,228k, more than a fifth of the plan's value, because the solver must fill each year exactly with whatever projects make the sums come out, valuable or not.

That is the general lesson about floors: a ceiling only ever removes plans, while a floor makes the model *fund work for its spend*, not its value. Set floors where the business really needs them, and report their cost.
A Jurisdiction's Spend Is the Same Sum Over Its Own Projects

A jurisdiction $`r`$ owns the projects $`P_r \subseteq P`$. Its spend in year $`y`$ is the year's spend expression summed over $`P_r`$ only, and its spend over the whole plan is simpler still: every GridCap project finishes inside the plan, so a funded project spends its whole capex there.
\sum_{i \in P_r} \text{capex}_i\, \text{started}(i) \;\ge\; F_r \qquad \forall r \in R \qquad \text{(floor}_r)

A **jurisdictional maximum** is the same row the other way round, $`\le U_r`$ over the plan, or a yearly one on the regional spend of each year, $`\sum_{i \in P_r} \sum_{t \le y} c_{i,y-t}\, x_{i,t} \le U_{r,y}`$. A minimum and a maximum on the same expression make a **band**. This lesson's GridCap runs use the regional floors; the maximum is the same row with the inequality reversed, and the first practice writes both.

`region_floors.py` prints each region's floor and the most it could ever receive, then solves with no floors, with GridCap's floors, and with the Plains floor raised to $8,000k, printing what each region receives:

floors             Ridge 3,130  Valley 4,300  Coast 4,110  Plains 2,410
most               Ridge 15,670  Valley 20,510  Coast 20,550  Plains 11,600
no floor           NPV $24,260k  Ridge 8,990  Valley 12,730  Coast 13,790  Plains 6,120
floors             NPV $24,260k  Ridge 8,990  Valley 12,730  Coast 13,790  Plains 6,120
Plains floor 8,000 NPV $23,837k  Ridge 7,270  Valley 7,050  Coast 19,420  Plains 8,150

GridCap's own floors cost nothing: every region already receives between two and a half and three and a half times its floor. The raised Plains floor costs $423k, and look at where the money comes from. Plains gains $2,030k, but Valley loses $5,680k, Ridge loses $1,720k and Coast gains $5,630k. A floor in one jurisdiction moves money between all the others, through the budgets they share, in ways no one would guess from the rule. Report every region's change when a floor moves, not only the region it names.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Share of the Plan Is Linear Once You Multiply Out the Total
"Vegetation is at least 8% of the plan's spend" looks like a ratio, and a ratio of two variable expressions is not linear:
\frac{\text{spend}_{\text{veg}}}{\text{spend}_{\text{all}}} \ge 0.08
But both sides can be multiplied by $`\text{spend}_{\text{all}}`$, which is never negative, so the inequality keeps its direction and becomes linear:
\text{spend}_{\text{veg}} \ge 0.08\, \text{spend}_{\text{all}} \qquad \text{(min\_share\_vegetation)}

The one case to think about is a plan that spends nothing: the ratio is undefined, and the linear row reads $`0 \ge 0`$, which allows it. That is almost always what the business means (an empty plan breaks no share rule), and here the must-dos make an empty plan impossible anyway.

Keep the share's own spend on the left. The reversed row, $`\text{spend}_{\text{all}} \ge 0.08\, \text{spend}_{\text{veg}}`$, says the total is at least 8% of the vegetation spend, which every plan meets, so it states no rule at all.

def at_least_share(plan, program, share):    # program spend >= share x total spend
    plan.model.add_linear_constraint(spend_of(plan, program) >= share * spend_of(plan), name=f"min_share_{program}")


def at_most_share(plan, program, share):     # program spend <= share x total spend
    plan.model.add_linear_constraint(spend_of(plan, program) <= share * spend_of(plan), name=f"max_share_{program}")

no share rule                  NPV $24,260k  spend $41,630k  transmission 64.2%  distribution 28.3%  vegetation 7.5%
vegetation at least 8%         NPV $24,146k  spend $41,860k  transmission 60.8%  distribution 30.6%  vegetation 8.6%
transmission at most 50%       NPV $23,328k  spend $40,980k  transmission 48.3%  distribution 44.1%  vegetation 7.6%
both                           NPV $23,135k  spend $40,570k  transmission 48.8%  distribution 43.0%  vegetation 8.2%

The vegetation rule costs $114k; the transmission cap costs $932k, because transmission holds the largest projects, and the plan cuts more than it has to (48.3%) since projects come whole. A share row is on the plan's *actual* spend, so it moves with the plan: under the transmission cap the plan spends $650k less in total than without it. A rule written as a share of the *budget* instead, $`\text{spend}_{\text{veg}} \ge 0.08 \sum_y B_y`$, is a different rule (a fixed floor), and it is a common mistake when the business says "share".
<!-- practice 2 -->
Floors Can Make the Model Infeasible: Check Them First, Knowing the Checks Are Not Enough

A ceiling alone never makes the model infeasible, since a plan that funds less always spends less; it takes a must-do or another row that forces spending. A floor can do it on its own: a jurisdiction cannot receive more than all of its projects cost. Two checks on the data catch the plain cases:

items: **Each floor against the most its jurisdiction can receive**: every project in it, but only the dearest option of each alternative group, since a plan funds at most one.
**The floors together against the budgets together.**

blocks.text: Valley's most, $20,510k, is less than all of its projects' capex ($21,530k), because of the alternative group G030. Now triple every floor:

floors x3 total $41,850k; precheck: no problem found
floors x3          INFEASIBLE

Both checks pass: each tripled floor is far below what its region could receive, and the floors total $41,850k against $42,230k of budgets. The model is still infeasible, because the floors must be met with whole projects, in the years their windows allow, under each year's own budget, with the must-dos and dependencies on top, and the last $380k of slack cannot absorb all of that. As in lesson 6.5.1, the checks are necessary, not sufficient. When they pass and the solver still says `INFEASIBLE`, lesson 9.1.4 relaxes the floors with penalized slack to find how far short the plan falls, which is often the number a regulator needs.
The Model
The planning model with this lesson's rows marked. Each program adds one family at a time.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the start years of project $`i`$; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$; $`R`$ the regions (jurisdictions), with $`P_r \subseteq P`$ the projects of region $`r`$; $`P_g \subseteq P`$ the projects of program $`g`$.

**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work, and $`\text{capex}_i = \sum_k c_{i,k}`$ ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k); $`\alpha \in [0, 1]`$, the floor's share of the budget; $`F_r`$ and $`U_r`$, region $`r`$'s floor and cap over the plan ($k); $`\underline{s}_g`$ and $`\bar{s}_g`$, program $`g`$'s least and most share of the plan's spend.

**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$; we write $`\text{started}(i) = \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t}`$, $`\text{spend}_y = \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t}`$, and $`S(Q) = \sum_{i \in Q} \text{capex}_i\, \text{started}(i)`$ for the plan's spend on a set of projects $`Q`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in g} \text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\textstyle\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \textstyle\sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\text{spend}_y &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y) \\
\text{spend}_y &\ge \alpha B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(floor}_y) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
\textstyle\sum_{y \in Y} \text{spend}_y &\ge \alpha \textstyle\sum_{y \in Y} B_y && && \text{(floor\_plan)} \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
S(P_r) &\ge F_r && \forall r \in R && \text{(floor}_r) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
S(P_r) &\le U_r && \forall r \in R && \text{(cap}_r) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson, the practice} \\
S(P_g) &\ge \underline{s}_g\, S(P) && \forall g && \text{(min\_share}_g) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
S(P_g) &\le \bar{s}_g\, S(P) && \forall g && \text{(max\_share}_g) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson}
\end{aligned}

`portfolio_spend.py` uses either the floor$`_y`$ rows or the floor\_plan row; `region_floors.py` the floor$`_r`$ rows; `program_share.py` the share rows for vegetation (at least 8%) and transmission (at most 50%).
Summary

items: **A spend limit is a row on a spend expression, from above or from below.** A floor makes the model fund work for its spend; spending every dollar cost $5,228k of NPV here.
**A jurisdiction's spend is the same sum over its own projects.** A floor in one region moved money between all the others; report every region's change.
**A share of the plan is linear once you multiply out the total.** Write it on the plan's actual spend, not on the budget.

**Floors can make the model infeasible: check them first, knowing the checks are not enough.** Each floor against its most, and all floors against all budgets; tripled floors passed both and were still infeasible.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: spend at most the budget in year $`y`$
spend at least $`\alpha`$ of each year's budget
spend at least $`\alpha`$ of the plan's budgets
jurisdiction $`r`$ gets at least $`F_r`$ / at most $`U_r`$ over the plan
jurisdiction $`r`$ gets at most $`U_{r,y}`$ in year $`y`$
program $`g`$ is at least / at most a share $`s`$ of the plan
it is above every project of its jurisdiction, one option per alternative group
they total more than all budgets
the must-dos inside it already spend more

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [MathOpt (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (models are built once and solved by any supported solver; this module uses HiGHS); [Integer Programming, Chapter 9 of Applied Mathematical Programming (MIT 15.053)](https://web.mit.edu/15.053/www/AMP-Chapter-09.pdf) (section 9.1: capital budgeting with a resource row per period, and cash-flow rows whose right side is the funds available in that period).
Challenges

items: Write the yearly floor as "at least 99% of each year's budget, or at least 99.5% of the plan's". Which variable do you need, and what does the solve cost?
In `region_floors.py`, find the largest Plains floor the plan can meet. Predict it before you search.
Rewrite "vegetation at least 8%" as a share of the budget, and compare the plan and its cost with the share of actual spend.

blocks.text: Design Note: Floors Come With Their Price

A floor is usually a promise someone made outside the model: a rate case, a municipal agreement, a board target. The model cannot judge it, but it can price it, by solving with and without the row (lesson 6.5.1) and by showing which jurisdictions paid for it. Ship every floor with that report. When a floor cannot be met, the right output is not a plan that quietly misses it, but the shortfall and its cause, which section 9 builds.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.
**portfolio_spend.py.** Adds yearly and plan-wide spend floors to GridCap small (*A Spend Limit Is a Row on a Spend Expression*). *Try:* Put the floor on 2030 alone, at 100%. Predict the cost.

**region_floors.py.** Holds each region above its floor, raises the Plains floor, checks tripled floors before the solve (*A Jurisdiction's Spend Is the Same Sum* and *Floors Can Make the Model Infeasible*). *Try:* Double the floors instead of tripling them. Predict whether the plan changes.

**program_share.py.** Bounds the vegetation and transmission shares of the plan's spend (*A Share of the Plan Is Linear Once You Multiply Out the Total*). *Try:* Require distribution to be at least 40%. Predict which program gives way.
**planning_model.py.** The model builder the programs import; `spend_by_year` builds the spend expressions.
